title: Control points: writing the check that shows a task is finished
moduleTitle: Group (Cleaning & Hygiene): Quality, evidence and handover
audience: Cleaners, leading hands and supervisors who write, follow or check task sheets for residential, commercial, bond, short-stay and strata work.
learningOutcomes: Write a control point as an observable check that a second person could confirm.
Link each control point to the step in the procedure that produces it.
Set a check frequency for shared and public areas, and name who records it.
Explain why a written site standard is a starting point that each site adapts.

instruction.heading: A standard is a first draft for your sites
instruction.body: A written cleaning manual describes what a job should look like, but it cannot see the building in front of you. The most useful way to use an inherited manual is to treat it as a first draft. The business keeps the parts that fit its sites, changes the parts that do not, and adds the checks its own customers expect. A standard only works when the people doing the work can see what it asks for. Before you adopt any set of task instructions, read it against the sites you actually clean and note where a step does not fit. Record the change, the reason for it and who approved it, so the next worker does not have to discover the same gap.

instruction.heading: What a control point is
instruction.body: A control point is a short statement, placed at the end of a task sheet or beside its steps, that says what must be true when the work is complete. It sits apart from the method. The method tells the worker what to do. The control point tells the worker and the checker what the result must look like. A good control point names a surface or area, a condition and a way to see that condition. A phrase such as looks clean fails this test, because two inspectors can disagree about what it means. A phrase that names the surface, the condition and the viewing position can be checked in a few seconds by anyone standing in the room.

instruction.heading: Writing checks that someone else can confirm
instruction.body: Start each control point from the finished surface and work backwards. Ask what a person entering the room would notice first, what a hand run along the surface would find, and what would show up under normal light. Prefer counts, positions and states. A bin is empty and its liner is fitted. A handrail has no marks along its full length. A floor has no standing water, and its warning sign comes down only once it is dry. Keep each control point to one condition, because two conditions in one line let a check pass when one of them has failed. If a check needs a tool, name the tool, such as a torch for checking streaks on glass, so the checker does not have to improvise.

instruction.heading: Linking each control point to the method
instruction.body: Every control point should trace back to a step. If the control point says the glass door panels are free of finger marks, a step must say when the glass is cleaned and with what. A control point with no step behind it is a gap in the standard. A step that produces nothing a control point checks may be unnecessary, or the check is missing. Walk the task from the first step to the last and mark which control point each step serves. Doing this on paper before a new task goes live catches most gaps. It also tells the worker which step to return to when a check fails, so the whole job does not have to be repeated.

instruction.heading: Check frequency in shared and public areas
instruction.body: Some areas need checks during the working day as well as at the end. Lobby glass, entrance doors, lifts and standing bins are seen by visitors throughout the day, so one end-of-shift check lets a marked state stand for hours. Set the frequency on the task sheet as a number of checks or a fixed interval, and name the person who records each check. Heavily used areas need more frequent checks. Where a customer or building manager has set a higher expectation, the business standard should reflect it. Frequency is a business decision that must be written down, not left to a worker's judgement on the day.

instruction.heading: Recording and acting on a failed check
instruction.body: A failed control point is information. Record which check failed, where it failed and what was found, then return to the step that produces that result. Do not sign off an area with a known failure, and do not quietly correct a result without recording it, because the record is how the business learns that a step is weak. If the same control point fails across different workers and sites, the problem is more likely to be the method or the equipment than the people, and it should go to the supervisor for review.

procedure: Read the task sheet and mark each step that changes a surface or a condition.
Check that each control point names a surface or area, a condition and a way to see it. Rewrite any that do not.
Trace each step to the control point it serves. Note any step with no check and any check with no step.
Set the check frequency for shared and public areas, and name the person who records each check.
At the end of the task, walk the area and check each control point in order, noting any failure.
For any failure, return to the matching step, correct the result, then record the failure, the fix and the time of the recheck.

workedExamples.situation: A small office has a glass entrance door, a reception desk and two shared kitchen benches. The task sheet says the area should look clean and be free of marks at the end of the shift.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Rewrite the entrance control point so that a second person can check it.
workedExamples.reasoning: State the surface, the condition and the way to see it. For example: the door panels show no finger marks or smears when viewed from inside the entrance and from the footpath side, and the handle has been wiped. Replace the word clean with a check that two people would agree on. Add a daytime check as well, because visitors touch the glass throughout the day.

workedExamples.situation: A bond clean in a two-bathroom unit. The bathroom control point says the taps are clean. The checker finds limescale at the base of one tap after the task is signed off.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What went wrong, and what should happen next?
workedExamples.reasoning: The control point did not name the part of the tap that needs checking, and it did not say how to check it. Reopen the task and return to the bathroom step that covers the basin and fittings. Clean the tap base, record the failure and the fix, then rewrite the control point to name the base, the spout and the handles, with a finger run along the base as the check.

workedExamples.situation: A strata lobby has a set of glass doors and a standing bin. The task sheet asks for one check at the end of the shift.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What check frequency would you put in the standard, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: One end-of-shift check lets visitors see the marks for the whole shift. Add a daytime check at an interval the supervisor approves, record who carries it out, and keep the end-of-shift check. The frequency is a business decision and needs to be written into the standard.

equipmentAndPpe: Task sheet or job card with the procedure steps and control points
Pen or tablet for recording checks
Torch or lamp for checking glass and shiny surfaces
Gloves and any other PPE the task sheet lists, when checking a surface by touch

commonErrors.error: Writing a control point that describes a feeling, such as looks clean or presentable.
commonErrors.prevention: Name the surface, the condition and the way to see it, so that a second person reaches the same result.

commonErrors.error: Putting two conditions into one control point.
commonErrors.prevention: Split the line so that each condition can pass or fail on its own.

commonErrors.error: Listing control points that no step produces.
commonErrors.prevention: Trace each control point back to a step, and add the missing step.

commonErrors.error: Signing off an area that has a known failure.
commonErrors.prevention: Return to the step, correct the result, record the failure and the fix, then check again before sign-off.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Control points do not replace the safety controls on the task sheet, such as warning signs and PPE. A surface that passes a visual check is not thereby safe to walk on or to touch with bare hands.
A customer contract or building requirement sets any frequency that it specifies.

The source for this lesson is a 2012 hospital cleaning manual. Its specific checks and its reference to a state health cleaning policy are not current requirements and have not been checked against current policy.

qualityStandard: Every control point names a surface or area, a condition and a way to see it.
Every step in the task produces a control point, and every control point traces back to a step.
Shared and public areas have a stated check frequency and a named person who records the checks.
A failed check is recorded with its fix before the area is signed off.
documentationEvidence: Task sheet showing the control points and the step that each one traces to.
Record of the check frequency for shared and public areas, with the person named.
Record of any failed check, the fix applied, and the time it was rechecked.
summary: A control point states what the finished work looks like and how it is seen.
Write checks that a second person can confirm, and trace each one to a step.
Set and record the check frequency for shared and public areas.
Record every failure and its fix before the area is signed off.

knowledgeChecks.question: A control point reads 'the bathroom looks clean'. Which change makes it checkable?
options: Add the word very so the standard sounds stronger and the bathroom looks finished
Name the surfaces, the condition and the way a second person would see it
Delete it, because appearance cannot be checked and leave the space blank

knowledgeChecks.question: After sign-off, a checker finds a dirty tap base. What should happen first?
options: Clean the tap base quietly and sign the area off again
Reopen the task, return to the basin step, and record the failure and the fix
Leave the area signed off and mention it at the next team meeting

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a lobby need a daytime check as well as an end-of-shift check?
options: Visitors see the glass and doors all day, so a marked state can last for hours
End-of-shift checks are valid only for the back-of-house areas and not for the lobby
A daytime check swaps for a weekly deep clean and the lobby is checked on Monday
